title: True realities bear the names of earthly things
source_text: Ὥσπερ δὲ αὐτὸς τὴν διήγησιν ἀνατίθεται τοῦ παρὰ Πλάτωνι μύθου, κειμένου (ἐν) τῷ Φαίδωνι. λέγων τάδε· τί δὲ διὰ τούτων ἐμφανίζει, οὐ παντὶ γνῶναι ῥᾴδιον· εἰ μὴ ὅστις ἐπαΐειν δύναιτο, τί ποτ᾿ ἐστὶν ἐκεῖνο ὅ φησιν· „ὑπ᾿ ἀσθενείας καὶ βραδυτῆτος οὐχ οἱους τε εἶναι διεξελθεῖν ἐπ᾿ ἔσχατον τὸν ἀέρα“· „καὶ εἰ ἡ φύσις ἱκανὴ εἴη ἀνασχέσθαι θεωροῦσα, γνῶναι ἂν ὅτι ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθῶς οὐρανὸς καὶ τὸ ἀληθινὸν φῶς“· τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ἡμεῖς τὰ περὶ τῆς ἁγίας καὶ ἀγαθῆς γῆς καὶ τῆς ἐν αὐτῇ πόλεως τοῦ θεοῦ οὐ κατὰ τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν νομίζοντες εἶναι πραγματείαν σαφηνίσαι ὑπερτιθέμεθα εἰς τὰ ἐξηγητικὰ τῶν προφητῶν, ἀπὸ μέρους κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν διηγησάμενοι περὶ πόλεως θεοῦ ἐν τοῖς πραγματευθεῖσιν ἡμῖν εἰς τὸν τεσσαρακοστὸν καὶ πέμπτον ψαλμὸν καὶ τὸν τεσσαρακοστὸν καὶ ἕβδομον ψαλμόν. οἶδε δὲ ὁ ἀρχαιότατος Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν λόγος τὰ ἀληθινὰ πάντα ὁμώνυμα τοῖς τῇδε καθολικωτέροις, οἷον „ἀληθινὸν φῶς“ καὶ „οὐρανὸν“ ἕτερον παρὰ „τὸ στερέωμα“ καὶ τὸν „τῆς δικαιοσύνης“ ἥλιον ἄλλον παρὰ τὸν αἰσθητόν. καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς δέ φησιν [ὅτι] πρὸς ἀντιδιαστολὴν τῶν αἰσθητῶν, ὧν οὐδέν ἐστιν ἀληθινὸν, τό· „θεὸς, ἀληθινὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ,“ ἐπ᾿ ἄλλων μὲν τάσσων τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπὶ ἡττόνων δὲ τὰ λεγόμενα „ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν“ αὐτοῦ. μεμφόμενος γοῦν τισι διὰ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου φησί· „τὰ ἔργα κυρίου οὐκ ἐμβλέπουσι καὶ τὰ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ οὐ κατανοοῦσι.“ καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον.
pass_a_gloss: Just as (ὥσπερ) he himself (Celsus) defers (ἀνατίθεμαι) the explanation (διήγησις) of the myth in Plato, lying in the Phaedo, saying this: ‘what he shows forth (ἐμφανίζω) through these is not easy for everyone to know, unless whoever could perceive (ἐπαΐω) what that is which he says: “by weakness (ἀσθένεια) and slowness (βραδυτής) we are not able to go through to the farthest air (ἀήρ)”; “and if nature (φύσις) were sufficient (ἱκανή) to endure (ἀνέχομαι) beholding (θεωρέω), it would know that that is the truly (ἀληθῶς) heaven and the true (ἀληθινόν) light (φῶς)”’; in the same way we too, not thinking the things about the holy and good land and the city of God in it to belong to the present treatise (πραγματεία), defer (ὑπερτίθεμαι) clarifying (σαφηνίζω) them to the exegetical works (ἐξηγητικά) on the prophets, having explained in part (ἀπὸ μέρους), as possible for us, about the city of God in our treatments (πραγματευθέντα) on the forty-fifth psalm and the forty-seventh psalm. The most ancient word (λόγος) of Moses and the prophets knows all the true things homonymous (ὁμώνυμα) with the more general/common (καθολικώτερα) things here, such as (οἷον) ‘true light’ and ‘heaven’ other than ‘the firmament (στερέωμα)’ and the sun ‘of righteousness (δικαιοσύνη)’ other than the sensible (αἰσθητός) one. And in a word it says, for distinction (ἀντιδιαστολή) from the sensibles, of which nothing is true, ‘God, true his works (ἔργα)’, assigning (τάσσω ἐπί) the works of God to some, and to lesser (ἥττονα) the so-called ‘works of his hands’. Blaming (μέμφομαι) some, at any rate, through Isaiah, it says: ‘the works of the Lord they do not look upon (ἐμβλέπω) and the works of his hands they do not consider (κατανοέω).’ And so much (ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον) for these.
pass_b_english: Celsus himself puts off the explanation of the myth in Plato, which is found in the Phaedo, saying: “What he means to show by these words is not easy for everyone to know, unless one were able to understand what it is that he says: ‘through weakness and slowness we are not able to pass through to the uttermost air’; and ‘if one’s nature were able to bear the sight, one would know that that is the true heaven and the true light’ (Plato, Phaedo 109d–110a).” In the same way we too, thinking that it does not belong to the present treatise to make clear what concerns the holy and good land and the city of God in it, put this off to our commentaries on the prophets. We have already given a partial account, as far as we could, of the city of God in what we have written on the forty-fifth Psalm and the forty-seventh Psalm (Psalms 46 and 48).

The most ancient teaching of Moses and the prophets knows that all the true things bear the same names as the more common things here. For example, it speaks of a “true light” (John 1:9), and a “heaven” other than “the firmament” (Genesis 1:1, 1:8), and a sun “of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2) other than the sun we perceive with the senses. And, in a word, to set them apart from the things of sense, none of which is true, it says: “God, true are his works” (Deuteronomy 32:4). It applies the name “works of God” to some things, and the so-called “works of his hands” to lesser ones. At any rate, when it reproaches certain people through Isaiah, it says: “They do not look upon the works of the Lord, and they do not consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5:12). So much for this.

choices.choice: The Greek subject of the first sentence is ‘he himself’ (αὐτός); ‘Celsus’ is supplied for clarity (Celsus quoted the Phaedo in the previous chapter). The words from ‘What he means to show’ to the end of the Plato extracts are Celsus’s, set in double quotation marks, with Plato’s words nested in single marks. The two Plato extracts run from Phaedo 109d to 110a (the first ends at 109d–e, the second is 109e–110a), so the inline citation gives the range. In the second extract the subject in Plato is ‘someone’ who reached the top; Origen’s text has only ‘nature’, so ‘one’s nature … one would know’ is used rather than ‘our’. ἀνατίθεται taken as ‘defers’, matching Origen’s own ὑπερτιθέμεθα that answers it. Origen’s psalm commentaries are named by LXX number (45 and 47), kept in the text, with English Psalms 46 and 48 in parentheses; these works are lost or fragmentary. Malachi 4:2 English = Malachi 3:20 LXX/Hebrew. Deuteronomy 32:4 follows the LXX (‘God, true are his works’; Hebrew ‘the Rock, his work is perfect’). ‘Heaven other than the firmament’ rests on Genesis 1:1 (heaven made) against 1:8 (the firmament named heaven); cited as an allusion. λόγος here is the teaching of Moses and the prophets, not the divine Word, so lower case. τοῖς τῇδε καθολικωτέροις rendered ‘the more common things here’ (things that commonly bear those names). Koetschau brackets ὅτι before the Deuteronomy quotation; not translated.
Plato citation corrected from ‘Phaedo 109e’ to ‘Phaedo 109d–110a’: the two extracts span that range
‘if our nature were able … it would know’ to ‘if one’s nature were able … one would know’: ‘our’ was not in the Greek and Plato’s subject is ‘someone’
οἷον rendered ‘For example, it speaks of’ instead of the weak ‘So there is’
‘It ranks the works of God among some things’ (stiff, from τάσσων ἐπί) to ‘It applies the name “works of God” to some things … to lesser ones’
Speaker frame checked: Celsus’s words in double marks, Plato nested in single marks; Deuteronomy 32:4 LXX, Malachi 4:2 (LXX 3:20), Isaiah 5:12, LXX Psalms 45/47 = 46/48 verified
